content.title: About
content.content: Sugar‑free cookie is a light, crunchy wafer made from whole grains, plant oils and sugar substitutes. It contains no added sugar but retains a mildly sweet taste thanks to natural sweeteners.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sugar‑free wafers are popular in diet plans and for people with diabetes.
Common sweeteners include stevia, erythritol or monk fruit extract.
The crisp texture is achieved by rapid baking at high temperature.
Products are often fortified with B‑vitamins and minerals such as iron and zinc.
Individually wrapped portions make calorie control convenient.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Absence of added sugar helps maintain stable blood glucose levels.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain ingredients provide fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: Plant oils supply monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fortification with B‑vitamins and minerals aids energy metabolism and immune function.

items.title: Weight‑management support
items.content: Low calorie density and lack of sugar make it suitable for weight‑control diets.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Formulations may contain nuts, soy or gluten, which require caution for allergic individuals.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some sugar substitutes can cause gastrointestinal discomfort when consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Calorie overconsumption
items.content: Although sugar‑free, the product still provides calories from fats and carbs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sugar‑free cookie can be enjoyed as a snack, added to yogurt, smoothies, or used in desserts as a substitute for regular wafers. Pairing with protein sources helps prolong satiety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For extended shelf life, store in the refrigerator to preserve crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Cottage cheese is a fresh, soft cheese made from the curds of milk. It has a mild, slightly tangy flavor and a creamy, lumpy texture. It is made by curdling milk with acid or rennet, draining the whey, and sometimes adding cream. It is available in low-fat and full-fat versions and is related to traditional fresh cheeses such as tvorog and quark.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cottage cheese is a fresh cheese, which means it is not aged.
It is sold with different curd sizes and fat levels, from fat-free to creamy.
Much of its protein is casein, which the body digests relatively slowly.
The liquid drained during production is called whey and is used in other foods.
Similar fresh curd cheeses are traditional in many countries across Europe and Asia.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Cottage cheese is a good source of protein, which supports muscle maintenance and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Provides calcium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals support normal bones and teeth.

items.title: Contains B vitamins
items.content: Cottage cheese contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin (B2), which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Versatile and filling
items.content: Its protein content makes it a satisfying addition to meals and snacks.

items.title: Lower in lactose than milk
items.content: Many fresh cheeses contain less lactose than milk, though the amount varies.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: People allergic to cow's milk protein should avoid cottage cheese.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cottage cheese still contains some lactose and may cause discomfort in people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some commercial products contain added salt, so people who limit sodium should check the label.

items.title: Spoilage
items.content: Fresh cheese spoils quickly. Avoid it if it has an off smell, sour taste beyond the usual tang, or visible mold.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cottage cheese can be eaten plain, with fruit, berries, honey, or nuts, or mixed with herbs, cucumbers, and tomatoes. It can be used in pancakes, dumplings, casseroles, pastries, dips, and as a filling. It also works well in smoothies and as a topping for toast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cottage cheese in the refrigerator in a tightly closed container. Use it within a few days after opening and always check the expiration date. Use a clean spoon each time to reduce contamination. Freezing can change the texture, so it is best suited for cooking afterward.

popcorn-popped-in-oil-no-butter-added.title: Popcorn popped in oil, no butter added

content.title: About
content.content: Popcorn is whole corn kernels that explode when heated, forming light, airy pieces. When prepared in vegetable oil without added butter, the natural corn flavor and the aroma of toasted oil are preserved.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is one of the oldest snacks; it was made by ancient civilizations in Mexico and Peru.
Each popcorn kernel contains about 14 % water; when heated, this water turns to steam and makes the kernel pop.
Oil‑popped popcorn without butter contains less saturated fat than traditional butter‑flavored popcorn.
Popcorn is a staple in movie theaters, but at home it can be made in a microwave, on the stovetop, or with a popcorn machine.
There are more than 30 corn varieties suitable for popping, but specially bred “popcorn” types give the best results.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: Popcorn contains virtually no sugar, making it a suitable snack for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: A 100‑g serving of popcorn provides about 14 g of dietary fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Corn polyphenols in popcorn have antioxidant properties that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low calorie when portioned
items.content: One cup of air‑popped popcorn has roughly 30 kcal; even when popped in a modest amount of oil, the calorie count remains moderate.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: The vegetable oil used adds monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn, ranging from skin rashes to severe symptoms.

items.title: High sodium if salted
items.content: Adding salt can make popcorn a source of excess sodium, which is undesirable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Burn risk
items.content: Hot oil and freshly popped kernels can cause burns, so handle the cooking process carefully.

items.title: Potential acrylamides
items.content: Over‑cooking in oil can produce acrylamides, potentially harmful compounds; aim for a golden‑yellow color instead of dark brown.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy popcorn as a standalone snack, or mix it with dried fruit, nuts, or spices. It pairs well with paprika, garlic powder, dried herbs, or a light sprinkle of sea salt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared popcorn in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For storage longer than a week, keep it in the refrigerator to prevent the oil from going rancid.

content.title: About
content.content: Black decaffeinated tea is a leaf tea made from Camellia sinensis whose caffeine has been removed. It retains the rich flavor of black tea while lacking the stimulating effect, making it suitable for those avoiding caffeine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeination is usually performed by steam or solvent methods, after which the leaves keep most of their aromatic compounds.
Decaf black tea is often used in evening rituals because it does not interfere with sleep.
Unlike green tea, black tea undergoes a longer oxidation process, giving it a stronger taste.
Decaffeinated tea may contain trace amounts of caffeine (typically less than 0.1 %).
In Russia and CIS countries, blends of decaf black tea with flavorings such as bergamot are popular.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Black tea contains polyphenols that help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Flavonoids in black tea improve vessel function and may lower the risk of hypertension.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Tannins stimulate gastric juice production, promoting better nutrient absorption.

items.title: Stress reduction
items.content: The aromatic profile of decaf black tea has a calming effect, helping to relax.

items.title: Immune system support
items.content: The tea provides B‑vitamins and minerals that contribute to normal immune function.

items.title: Tea allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to components of the tea leaf.

items.title: Tannin content
items.content: High tannin levels can reduce iron absorption, so people with anemia should drink tea between meals.

items.title: Residual solvents
items.content: When solvents are used for decaffeination, choose products that meet strict quality controls to avoid chemical residues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steep 1‑2 tsp of leaves in 200 ml of hot (not boiling) water for 3‑5 minutes. Enjoy plain or with a touch of honey, lemon, or milk to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the tea in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Keep it away from moisture and strong odors to preserve flavor and aroma.
